title: Numbers Below Zero
text: Negative numbers describe values below a chosen zero. A temperature of minus five degrees is five degrees below zero; a debt of five dollars can also be represented by negative five. Multiplying two negative numbers gives a positive because reversing direction twice restores the original direction.
context: A conceptual introduction to negative numbers.
vocabulary: represented: shown in another form
direction: the course along which something moves

title: Why Pi Appears
text: Divide the circumference of any circle by its diameter and the result is always pi, approximately 3.14159. A large circle and a tiny circle share this ratio. Pi's decimal digits never settle into a repeating pattern, yet the number lets us calculate circular lengths, areas, waves, and rotations.
context: A simplified introduction to the constant pi.
vocabulary: circumference: distance around a circle
diameter: line through a circle's center

title: A Square on Every Side
text: For a right triangle, the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. Written compactly, a² + b² = c². The relationship helps calculate distances that are difficult to measure directly, from a diagonal across a room to a point on a coordinate grid.
context: A conceptual explanation of the Pythagorean theorem.
vocabulary: diagonal: a line joining nonadjacent corners
coordinate: a number locating a point

title: Chance and Evidence
text: Probability measures uncertainty from zero, meaning impossible, to one, meaning certain. If a fair coin is tossed many times, heads should approach one half of the results, but a short run may look uneven. Probability predicts long-run patterns; it does not promise a tidy sequence today.
context: An introduction to theoretical and experimental probability.
vocabulary: uncertainty: lack of certainty
long-run: considered over many repetitions

title: More Than One Infinity
text: Infinity is not an ordinary number waiting at the end of counting. Georg Cantor compared infinite sets by pairing their members. Every whole number can be paired with an even number, yet real numbers cannot be paired with whole numbers in the same way. This reveals different sizes of infinity.
context: A simplified glimpse of Cantor's set theory.
vocabulary: set: a collection of distinct objects
paired: matched one-to-one

title: Measuring Change Now
text: Average speed compares a whole distance with a whole time. Calculus asks for speed at a single instant. A derivative answers by examining average changes over smaller and smaller intervals. The intervals approach zero without becoming a division by zero, allowing a curve's changing slope to be described precisely.
context: A conceptual introduction to derivatives and limits.
vocabulary: derivative: a measure of instantaneous change
interval: the space between two values

title: A Variable Is a Useful Name
text: A variable is a letter or symbol that stands for a number. In x + 5 = 12, the equation says that one unknown number plus five equals twelve, so x is seven. Variables can also describe changing quantities. If t is time, then a formula can show how distance depends on t. The symbol is a useful name, not a trick.
context: A concrete distinction between an unknown in an equation and a changing quantity in a formula.
vocabulary: variable: a symbol representing a number
equation: a statement that two expressions are equal
source: Original summary based on OpenStax, Elementary Algebra 2e, Use a General Strategy to Solve Linear Equations

references.citation: OpenStax, Elementary Algebra 2e, Use a General Strategy to Solve Linear Equations

title: Prime Building Blocks
text: A prime number is a whole number greater than one with exactly two positive factors: one and itself. Every whole number greater than one can be written as a product of primes. For example, 60 equals 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Apart from order, this prime factorization is unique. That makes primes like building blocks for multiplication. The number one is not prime, because including it would destroy the useful uniqueness of the factorization.
context: An intuitive introduction to primes and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.
vocabulary: factor: a number multiplied by another to make a product
unique: the only one of its kind
source: Original summary based on OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, Prime Factorization and the Least Common Multiple

references.citation: OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, Prime Factorization and the Least Common Multiple

title: Logarithms Ask for the Exponent
text: An exponent answers a multiplication question: 10 cubed is 1,000. A logarithm reverses that question. The base-10 logarithm of 1,000 is 3 because three is the exponent placed on 10. This reversal makes logarithms useful when quantities span enormous ranges or grow by repeated multiplication. Before electronic calculators, logarithm tables turned difficult multiplication into addition. The idea is exact, while a decimal approximation of a logarithm may be rounded. Thinking of logarithms as inverse exponents removes much of their mystery.
context: A simplified but mathematically accurate explanation of logarithms as inverse operations.
vocabulary: inverse: an operation that reverses another
approximation: a value close to, but not exactly, the true value
source: Original summary based on OpenStax, College Algebra 2e, Logarithmic Functions

title: Counting Teams Without Listing Them
text: Suppose a coach must choose three players from ten, and the order of their names does not matter. Listing every team would be slow and might repeat groups. Combinations provide a systematic count. First imagine ordered choices: ten options, then nine, then eight. That gives 720 arrangements. Each three-person team appears six times because its members can be ordered in 3 × 2 × 1 ways. Dividing 720 by 6 gives 120 different teams. The formula is a compressed version of this reasoning, not a rule that appeared from nowhere.
context: A worked intuition for combinations that explains why division by the ordering count is required.
vocabulary: combination: a selection in which order does not matter
systematic: done by a complete, organized method
source: Original summary based on OpenStax, Contemporary Mathematics, Counting Methods

title: A Limit Describes an Approach
text: A limit asks what value a function approaches as its input moves close to a chosen number. Imagine f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1). At x = 1, this expression has zero in the denominator and is undefined. Yet whenever x is not 1, factoring shows that it equals x + 1. As x approaches 1 from either side, the output approaches 2. Therefore the limit is 2 even though the original function has a hole there. A limit is not merely substituting the final input; it describes nearby behavior with a precise definition. This idea allows calculus to discuss instantaneous change and accumulated area without pretending that division by zero is allowed.
context: A standard removable-discontinuity example distinguishing a limit from a function value.
vocabulary: function: a rule assigning one output to each allowed input
undefined: not assigned a valid mathematical value
source: Original summary based on OpenStax, Calculus Volume 1, The Limit of a Function

references.citation: OpenStax, Calculus Volume 1, The Limit of a Function

title: Clock Arithmetic and Secret Messages
text: Modular arithmetic tracks remainders after division. On a twelve-hour clock, adding five hours to 10 gives 3, because 15 and 3 leave the same remainder when divided by 12. Mathematicians write this relationship as 15 ≡ 3 (mod 12). The idea creates repeating number systems that are useful far beyond clocks. In basic cryptography, a letter can become a number and be shifted by a fixed amount modulo 26; wrapping around keeps every result in the alphabet. Modern encryption uses much more difficult operations, so a simple shift is not secure. Still, the example reveals the foundation: arithmetic rules can transform information predictably for someone who knows the key, while making the pattern less obvious to an observer.
context: A precise introduction to congruence and a clearly limited toy example from cryptography.
vocabulary: remainder: what is left after whole-number division
cryptography: methods for protecting information with codes and mathematics
source: Original summary based on OpenStax, Contemporary Mathematics, Number Theory and Cryptography
